summary: An excerpt from Book 11 (part 137) of the story, in which Rebecca comforts her mother Aurelia, who lies ill in bed and despairs that all the family's sacrifices for Rebecca's education and prospects have been wasted. Rebecca answers with optimism, comparing herself to a young tree in its rooting season and playfully claiming to be a princess in disguise whose kingdom will one day be handed to her. Aurelia is partly comforted but worries about the family's hardships, including Aunt Miranda's crippled state, her own confinement, and the children Jenny, Fanny and Mark.
one_line: Rebecca cheers her bedridden mother Aurelia, who despairs that the family's sacrifices for Rebecca's future have come to nothing.
key_facts: Aurelia covers her eyes and cries, 'I can't bear it!' because she is chained to her bed and interfering with Rebecca's plans.
Aurelia lists the family's sacrifices as 'All my saving and doing without; all your hard study; all Mirandy's outlay.'
Rebecca sits down impetuously on the floor by the bed and tells her mother 'I'm only a little past seventeen.'
Rebecca compares herself to a young tree that John transplanted, which did not grow during a dry summer and a cold winter but made up for lost time in a good year.
Rebecca calls her current state 'my little rooting season' and says her day has not yet begun.
Rebecca notes that the old maple by the well, in its hundredth year, had new leaves that summer, so 'there must be hope for me at seventeen.'
Aurelia says Rebecca has 'lost your place' and 'you'll never see your friends here', calling her 'nothing but a drudge'.
Rebecca jokingly claims to be 'a princess' wearing 'a disguise' for 'reasons of state', with the king and queen 'going to abdicate shortly in my favor'.
Rebecca says the kingdom is 'rather a small kingdom' and imagines a throne 'of ivory with a nice screen of peacock feathers for a background'.
Rebecca promises her mother 'a comfortable chair very near it' with slaves to perform her 'lightest bidding'.
Aurelia smiles in spite of herself and is comforted, though not wholly deceived.
Aurelia says life looks 'very hard and rough' to her, citing Aunt Miranda as 'a cripple at the brick house' and herself as 'another here at the farm'.
Aurelia names Jenny, Fanny and Mark as further burdens tying Rebecca 'hand and foot'.
Aurelia tells Rebecca she has 'something of your father's happy disposition'.
Rebecca declares, 'it's enough joy just to be here in the world on a day like this'.
